passages.title: The Shivering Sand
passages.text:
Our house is high up on the Yorkshire coast, and close by the sea. We have got beautiful walks all round us, in every direction but one. That one I acknowledge to be a horrid walk. It leads, for a quarter of a mile, through a melancholy plantation of firs, and brings you out between low cliffs on the loneliest and ugliest little bay on all our coast.

The sandhills here run down to the sea, and end in two spits of rock jutting out opposite each other, till you lose sight of them in the water. One is called the North Spit, and one the South. Between the two, shifting backwards and forwards at certain seasons of the year, lies the most horrible quicksand on the shores of Yorkshire. At the turn of the tide, something goes on in the unknown deeps below, which sets the whole face of the quicksand shivering and trembling in a manner most remarkable to see, and which has given to it, among the people in our parts, the name of the Shivering Sand. A great bank, half a mile out, nigh the mouth of the bay, breaks the force of the main ocean coming in from the offing. Winter and summer, when the tide flows over the quicksand, the sea seems to leave the waves behind it on the bank, and rolls its waters in smoothly with a heave, and covers the sand in silence. A lonesome and a horrid retreat, I can tell you! No boat ever ventures into this bay. No children from our fishing-village, called Cobb's Hole, ever come here to play. The very birds of the air, as it seems to me, give the Shivering Sand a wide berth. That a young woman, with dozens of nice walks to choose from, and company to go with her, if she only said "Come!", should prefer this place, and should sit and work or read in it, all alone, when it's her turn out, I grant you, passes belief. It's true, nevertheless, account for it as you may, that this was Rosanna Spearman's favourite walk, except when she went once or twice to Cobb's Hole, to see the only friend she had in our neighbourhood, of whom more anon. It's also true that I was now setting out for this same place, to fetch the girl in to dinner, which brings us round happily to our former point, and starts us fair again on our way to the sands.

I saw no sign of the girl in the plantation. When I got out, through the sandhills, on to the beach, there she was, in her little straw bonnet, and her plain grey cloak that she always wore to hide her deformed shoulder as much as might be -- there she was, all alone, looking out on the quicksand and the sea.

She started when I came up with her, and turned her head away from me. Not looking me in the face being another of the proceedings, which, as head of the servants, I never allow, on principle, to pass without inquiry -- I turned her round my way, and saw that she was crying. My bandanna handkerchief -- one of six beauties given to me by my lady -- was handy in my pocket. I took it out, and I said to Rosanna, "Come and sit down, my dear, on the slope of the beach along with me. I'll dry your eyes for you first, and then I'll make so bold as to ask what you have been crying about."
passages.source_note: Public domain: from The Moonstone by Wilkie Collins (1868). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: When the narrator comes up to Rosanna, she turns her face from him. The passage suggests she does this because she

options.text: has not noticed that he has arrived
does not want him to see that she has been crying
is watching a boat out on the great bank
is angry that he has come to fetch her
is pointing something out across the water

questions.explanation: As soon as he turns her round he sees 'that she was crying'; turning away is her attempt to hide her tears, which he then quietly draws out.

questions.stem: What are the two spits of rock called?

options.text: The East Spit and the West
The High Spit and the Low
Cobb's Hole and the offing
The North Spit and the South
The great bank and the main ocean

questions.explanation: The passage states: 'One is called the North Spit, and one the South.'

questions.stem: Betteredge lists everything that stays away from the bay -- boats, children, even the birds -- just before saying Rosanna chose to sit there. What does putting these two things side by side do?

options.text: It proves the bay is a safe harbour in a storm
It makes Rosanna's fondness for the spot seem the stranger
It shows the fishing-village had grown too large
It suggests the birds were frightened of the tide
It hints that Rosanna is about to be sent away

questions.explanation: Setting the list of who avoids the bay right against Rosanna's choosing it throws her preference into relief -- the text follows straight on with 'That a young woman... should prefer this place... passes belief.'

questions.stem: The narrator says the birds give the sand 'a wide berth'. Here 'berth' refers to a

options.text: place to sleep on a ship
harbour for boats
space kept clear of
birth or beginning
nest built in the sand

questions.explanation: 'Give a wide berth' means to keep well clear of; here 'berth' means a space kept between the birds and the sand.

questions.stem: What is the effect of describing the sand as 'shivering and trembling'?

options.text: It makes the sand seem alive and unsettling
It suggests the sand is cold to the touch
It tells us the weather is stormy
It shows the sand is being blown by wind
It proves the sand is perfectly still

questions.explanation: Giving the sand human actions ('shivering and trembling') makes it feel eerily alive, adding to the menace of the place.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the opening paragraph about the 'horrid walk'?

options.text: To describe the quicksand in close detail
To lead the reader from the house towards the bay
To introduce Rosanna's crying on the beach
To explain the legend behind the sand's name
To list the beautiful walks around the house

questions.explanation: The first paragraph moves us from the house, through the plantation, out to the bay -- setting the scene before the sand itself is described.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the whole extract is organised?

options.text: It jumps back and forth between two different days
It argues a point and then gives three proofs
It lists events strictly in the order a diary would
It compares the Yorkshire coast with another county
It moves from a wide description of the place to a single person met there

questions.explanation: The extract opens on the walk and bay in general, narrows to the quicksand, then closes on the narrator finding one person -- Rosanna -- there.

questions.stem: What does Rosanna's choice of walk suggest about her?

options.text: She is cheerful and enjoys busy places
She is frightened of the sea and avoids it
She prefers to be alone rather than with company
She does not know the other walks exist
She only visits the bay when ordered to

questions.explanation: She chooses this lonely spot over 'dozens of nice walks' and 'company', and sits there 'all alone' -- pointing to a solitary nature.

questions.stem: The exclamation 'A lonesome and a horrid retreat, I can tell you!' mainly conveys the narrator's

options.text: secret admiration of the view
strong distaste for the place
boredom with telling the story
fear of being punished
delight at the coming tide

questions.explanation: The words 'lonesome', 'horrid' and the emphatic 'I can tell you!' show Betteredge's clear dislike of the spot.

questions.stem: What is the name of the fishing-village mentioned in the passage?

options.text: The North Spit
Yorkshire Bay
Cobb's Hole
The Shivering Sand
The offing

questions.explanation: The passage names the fishing-village as 'Cobb's Hole'.

questions.stem: When Betteredge says a young woman preferring the place 'passes belief', he means it

options.text: happens all the time
is a well-known local rule
has been proved false
takes only a moment
is very hard to believe

questions.explanation: 'Passes belief' means it goes beyond what one can believe -- Betteredge finds her preference hard to credit.

questions.stem: The passage says something 'sets the whole face of the quicksand shivering'. What device gives the sand a 'face'?

options.text: Simile
Onomatopoeia
Personification
Alliteration
Hyperbole

questions.explanation: Giving the sand a 'face' -- a human feature -- is personification.

questions.stem: What has just happened when the narrator reaches the beach?

options.text: He has found Rosanna standing there in tears
He has thrown a stone into the quicksand
He has been called away by a shouting voice
He has lost sight of Rosanna in the firs
He has sat down to rest after a long swim

questions.explanation: He gets out onto the beach, sees Rosanna alone, and turning her round finds 'that she was crying'.

questions.stem: Why does Betteredge describe the bay at length before letting Rosanna appear on it?

options.text: Because he cannot remember the order that events happened
So the reader already feels the place's gloom when she is found there
To hide from the reader that Rosanna is crying
Because the bay matters more to the plot than any person
To pad out a story he finds dull to tell

questions.explanation: Setting the eerie scene first means the reader carries its dread into the moment Rosanna is discovered alone and weeping there.

questions.stem: What was Rosanna wearing when the narrator found her?

options.text: A beautiful fawn-coloured suit
A bandanna handkerchief round her head
A sailor's coat and heavy boots
Nothing but her working apron
A little straw bonnet and a plain grey cloak

questions.explanation: The text describes her 'in her little straw bonnet, and her plain grey cloak'.

questions.stem: In 'a melancholy plantation of firs', the word 'melancholy' suggests the firs are

options.text: crowded
ancient
fragrant
golden
gloomy

questions.explanation: 'Melancholy' means sad or gloomy; the firs give the walk a dismal air.

questions.stem: Which quotation best shows that the sea arrives quietly rather than crashing in?

options.text: 'rolls its waters in smoothly with a heave, and covers the sand in silence'
'the most horrible quicksand on the shores of Yorkshire'
'breaks the force of the main ocean coming in from the offing'
'end in two spits of rock jutting out opposite each other'
'something goes on in the unknown deeps below'

questions.explanation: The phrase 'rolls its waters in smoothly... and covers the sand in silence' directly shows the sea coming in quietly.

questions.stem: Which phrase from the passage is the clearest example of alliteration?

options.text: 'loneliest and ugliest little bay'
'shifting backwards and forwards'
'certain seasons of the year'
'company to go with her'
'turned her head away'

questions.explanation: 'Loneliest' and 'little' repeat the same 'l' sound close together, which is alliteration.

questions.stem: Why does Betteredge pause to tell us his handkerchief was 'one of six beauties given to me by my lady'?

options.text: To prove the handkerchief was the wrong colour for Rosanna
To explain why Rosanna refused to stop crying
To warn that the handkerchief would soon be lost
To show, in passing, how proud and valued a servant he is
To describe the fashion of the fishing-village

questions.explanation: The proud aside about a gift from his lady quietly flags Betteredge's sense of his own standing, colouring how he narrates.

questions.stem: Which of these happens LAST in the passage?

options.text: The tide flows over the quicksand
Betteredge walks through the plantation of firs
The great bank breaks the force of the ocean
Betteredge offers Rosanna his handkerchief
Rosanna is named as fond of this walk

questions.explanation: The offer of the handkerchief and the words 'Come and sit down' come at the very end of the extract.

questions.stem: Betteredge calls the walk 'horrid'. Which word keeps most closely to the sense he intends here?

options.text: untidy
rocky
dreadful
chilly
crowded

questions.explanation: He means the walk is dreadful and unpleasant to him -- not merely untidy or cold; 'dreadful' matches that shade.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what gives the quicksand the name 'the Shivering Sand'?

options.text: The way its whole face shivers and trembles at the turn of the tide
The cold winds that blow across it in winter
The boats that once sank there long ago
The children who shivered with fear beside it
The grey cloak Rosanna wore on the beach

questions.explanation: The name comes because, at the turn of the tide, the sand's 'whole face' is set 'shivering and trembling'.

questions.stem: Why does Betteredge turn Rosanna 'round my way'?

options.text: Because she asked him to dry her eyes
Because the tide was about to reach her feet
Because he wanted her to see the North Spit
Because he will not let not looking him in the face pass without inquiry
Because dinner was already on the table

questions.explanation: He explains that, as head of the servants, he never lets someone avoiding his face 'pass without inquiry', so he turns her round.

questions.stem: In 'her deformed shoulder', what part of speech is 'deformed'?

options.text: Verb
Adverb
Noun
Adjective
Pronoun

questions.explanation: Here 'deformed' describes the noun 'shoulder', so it works as an adjective, even though it comes from a verb.

questions.stem: The sea rolls its waters in 'smoothly'. What part of speech is 'smoothly' here?

options.text: Adjective
Adverb
Noun
Verb
Preposition

questions.explanation: 'Smoothly' describes how the sea 'rolls' its waters, so it is an adverb modifying the verb.
